amendments.rule: An article in attributive position governs its head noun across whatever stands between them, so an interposed genitive does not turn it into something else. `τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν χάριτα` → *the grace of our God* and `περὶ τοῦ Μωϋσέως σώματος` → *about the body of Moses* give the English *the* to the outer article under rules 19 and 21, and the interposed genitive stands on its own English word, as `ὁ τοῦ κόσμου ἄρχων` → *the prince of the world* and `τῆς τοῦ κόσμου ζωῆς` → *the life of the world* do. The head noun is then bare, and the supplied-determiner clause of rule 51 does not apply to it, because an article is present to take that determiner. Rule 23's article before a name is the contrast and it is a narrow one: it applies where the name **is** the article's head noun, as `τοῦ Ἰησοῦ` → *of Jesus* is. So do not read an article as standing before a name merely because a name follows it, and do not decide the question from a morph string — a form-ambiguous `τοῦ`, `τῷ` or `τῶν` can be tagged for the interposed word rather than for the noun it actually governs, and the construction decides. Rules 20, 38, 47 and 49 are untouched: where a possessive, a demonstrative or an English *'s* already occupies the determiner slot the article is `unrepresented` as they say, which is why `τῆς Καίσαρος οἰκίας` → *Caesar's household* leaves it empty, and where the ASV supplies no determiner at all rule 23 does. An article that follows its noun is rule 31's case, not this one. Where the genitive carries **an article of its own**, that inner article is decided separately and on its own phrase, and the ASV's placement of the possessor decides both. Where the possessor stands **before** the head — the English prenominal possessive with *'s* that rule 20 already names as a displacer — the inner article takes the determiner the ASV writes on the possessor and the genitive takes only the possessive word: `τὸ τοῦ ἑτέρου` → *his neighbor's good* gives *his* to the inner article and *neighbor's* to the genitive, and `τὴν τοῦ ἑτέρου` → *the other's* gives *the* to the inner article and *other's* to the genitive. The outer article is then `unrepresented` under rule 20, its determiner slot being occupied, unless the ASV supplies a nominal for it, which it takes under rule 102 — which is why the same `τὸ τοῦ ἑτέρου` keeps *good* on the outer article and nothing else. Where the possessor stands **after** the head nothing is displaced and each article takes its own determiner in the ordinary way, so `τὸ τῶν πολλῶν` → *the profit of the many* gives *the profit* to the outer article under rule 102 and *of the* to the inner under rule 21. Do not empty the inner article in order to hand the outer one the *the* that the English writes on the possessor: a possessive phrase's determiner determines the possessor, and rule 20 has already emptied the article that possessive displaced. A determinerless English possessor is untouched by this and is rule 21's case, so `τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ` → *the things of God* leaves the inner article `unrepresented` and keeps *of* with the noun.
amendments.why: 1 Corinthians 10 writes the same τὸ τοῦ ἑτέρου twice, at 10:24 and 10:29, and the chapter analysed the inner article two ways because rule 57 says what the outer article does with an interposed genitive and nothing about the genitive's own article. Rule 20 already empties an article whose determiner slot an English 's occupies, and rule 102 already gives an article a supplied nominal; what was missing is that the determiner the English writes on the possessor belongs to the possessor's own article, which is what emptied the wrong one of the two here. The amendment adds only that nesting clause, with the chapter's own three shapes as its examples, and scopes it to a prenominal possessive so that τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ → 'the things of God' and the rule's existing examples are untouched. Written as an amendment rather than a new rule because rule 57 is the sentence a verse pass reads when it meets this construction, and a cross-reference left in its place would leave the gap where the error happened.

conventions: Doubled article with a genitive possessor (τὸ τοῦ ἑτέρου at 10:24, τὴν τοῦ ἑτέρου at 10:29, τὸ τῶν πολλῶν at 10:33): where the ASV renders the possessor prenominally with 's, the inner article takes the determiner the English writes on the possessor ('his' at 10:24, 'the' at 10:29), the genitive takes only the possessive word, and the outer article is unrepresented under rule 20 unless the ASV supplies a nominal for it, which it takes under rule 102 ('good' at 10:24). Where the possessor follows the head ('of the many' at 10:33) nothing is displaced and each article takes its own determiner.

Substantival article with a reflexive genitive (τὸ ἑαυτοῦ at 10:24, τὴν ἑαυτοῦ at 10:29, τὸ ἐμαυτοῦ at 10:33): the reflexive carries the English possessive ('his', 'thine', 'mine') and the article carries the supplied nominal 'own'. Emptying the article and folding 'own' onto the reflexive is the competing reading and was rejected in all three verses.

Substantival article whose complement is an adjective recast as an English relative clause: the relativizer follows the verb. Where the adjective's own English stays adjectival and only a copula is supplied, the article keeps the relativizer and the adjective takes the copula — οἱ πολλοί → 'we who' / 'are many' at 10:17 (rules 22, 53). Where the adjective's own English is a lexical verb, that verb carries the relativizer — τῶν ἀπίστων → 'of them' / 'that believe not' at 10:27 (rules 31, 32), the case preposition riding with the article. Rule 22's carve-out names only a following participle and does not by itself decide an adjective.

Supplied English in this chapter was decided by whether some token's own English is still incomplete, not by the ASV's italics: 'I say' at 10:20 is added because no token licenses it (rules 5, 86), while 'to a feast' folds onto καλεῖ at 10:27, the repeated 'for … sake' onto συνείδησιν at 10:28 (rules 86, 103), and the italic 'good' and 'profit' onto their own articles at 10:24 and 10:33 (rule 102).

report: One real cross-verse split: the doubled article of τὸ/τὴν τοῦ ἑτέρου, analysed one way at 10:24 (τοῦ → 'his', the determiner the English writes on the possessor) and the other way at 10:29 (τοῦ → unrepresented, τήν → 'the'). In 'the other's' the 'the' determines 'other', so it belongs to the inner article, and the outer article — head noun elided, determiner slot occupied by the possessive — is what rule 20 empties, exactly as it empties the article of τῆς Καίσαρος οἰκίας → 'Caesar's household'. The ASV's own note at 10:24 glosses τοῦ ἑτέρου as 'the other's', the same two words. Patched 10:29 only.

10:33's τὸ τῶν πολλῶν → 'the profit of the many' is not a third treatment and needs no patch: the possessor stands after the head, nothing is displaced, and each article keeps its own determiner under rules 21 and 102.

Checked and found licensed rather than split: οἱ πολλοί → 'we who' / 'are many' (10:17) against τῶν ἀπίστων → 'of them' / 'that believe not' (10:27) — the relativizer follows the verb, the first adjective's own English staying adjectival with only a supplied copula (rules 22, 53) while the second's own English is a lexical verb (rules 31, 32); and τὸν μηνύσαντα → 'that' (10:28) against 'that eat' / 'that thinketh' (10:12, 10:18), which is rule 90's one-word-versus-two-words test, ἐκεῖνον having taken the pronoun slot.

Also checked across verses: πᾶν τό → 'whatsoever' with the article empty at 10:25 and 10:27 (rule 80); 'for … sake' on διά at 10:25/27/28 with the repeated frame folded onto συνείδησιν (rules 86, 103); preverb particles at 10:1, 10:7 and 10:27 (rule 106); light-verb heads on the complement at 10:8, 10:9, 10:12, 10:22 and 10:30, and on the verb word at 10:30's βλασφημοῦμαι (rule 91); supplied determiners on anarthrous nouns through 10:21 and 10:4's discontinuous 'a … rock' (rules 51, 58); article before a name and before θεός unrepresented throughout (rule 23).

Read the dump end to end for the case the lemma table is blind to. The two added units at 10:20 ('I say', a matrix verb no token licenses, rules 5 and 86; 'the Gentiles', the excluded fallback at v017, rule 97) are consistent with the folds elsewhere in the chapter ('to a feast' onto καλεῖ at 10:27, the repeated 'for … sake' onto συνείδησιν at 10:28, the italic 'good' and 'profit' onto their articles at 10:24 and 10:33): the test applied throughout is whether some token's own English is still incomplete.

BSB: none of the three is an error. 10.6 τό is the nominalizing article of an articular infinitive, unrepresented in rule 61's own terms; 10.22 μή is interrogative, and rule 44 says in terms that the report is not a correction; 10.29 τοῦ is the genuine finding above. Fixing it moves the disagreement onto τήν rather than removing it, since three source tokens meet two English words either way, so the aggregate is unchanged and nothing was moved to improve it.

Promotion: one amendment, to rule 57, which already governs an article with an interposed genitive and already says the outer article empties where an English 's takes its slot, but never says what the genitive's own article gets. That silence is what the verse pass fell into. The adjective-relativizer judgment is logged as a convention and not promoted: it rests on one instance per side with no corpus check, and a weak rule is paid for by every chapter after this one.
